The 23 substances defining exposure include methamphetamine, amphetamine, MDMA and MDA; no breakdown by substance is given. Adjustment: age, sex and five comorbidity diagnoses (depression, anxiety, ischaemic heart disease, cardiovascular disease, stroke) recorded at any time during 2007–2016; nothing for other drug or alcohol use, socio-economic position or family history. Outcome codes listed: 295, 296.04, 296.14, 296.24, 296.34, 296.44, 296.54 and 296.64 (mood disorders with psychotic features), 297, 298.0, 298.1, 298.4, 298.8, 298.9 and 780.1; the drug-induced psychosis codes 292.1, 292.11 and 292.12 appear only in the exclusion list, although the text says other stimulant use disorders with psychosis were included. The authors state that the analysis was not preregistered and should be considered exploratory.

By number of arrests, counted from the index date to the end of the study, adjusted HRs: one 4.49 (4.09–4.93), two 5.07, three 5.24, four 5.53, five or more 6.25 (5.42–7.20); p for trend 0.038, printed in the incidence-rate column, which a linear regression of the five category rates on the number of arrests reproduces (editors' calculation). Person-years per person rise from about 4.4 with one arrest to 6.5 with five or more (editors' calculation). The authors state that the database has no validated measures of dose, frequency, amount or severity, so dose dependence could not be asserted, that arrests reflect police activity and priorities and do not capture all use (many people who use are never arrested), that the comparison group may include people who use amphetamines, and that people who use more often may be more likely to be arrested.
